name: TCAN4550RGYRQ1
title: Automotive CAN FD system basis chip: controller, transceiver and SPI host interface
summary: The TCAN4550-Q1 puts a complete CAN FD node behind a four-wire SPI port: a Bosch M_CAN revision 3.2.1.1 protocol controller with 2 KB of message RAM, and a high-speed CAN FD transceiver good for 8 Mbps, run from a battery supply of 5.5 V to 30 V. An on-chip 5 V regulator feeds the transceiver and offers up to 70 mA on VCCOUT to other parts, while the logic side follows a 3.3 V or 5 V VIO rail. It has normal, standby and sleep modes, wake-up from the bus (ISO 11898-2:2016 wake-up pattern) or from a high-voltage WAKE pin, an INH output that switches the node's regulator, a watchdog, failsafe timers, and bus pins rated ±58 V. It is AEC-Q100 grade 1 (–40 °C to 125 °C) in a 3.5 mm × 4.5 mm 20-pin VQFN.
key_figures: 5.5 V to 30 V (42 V abs max)

pins.name: OSC1
pins.function: Crystal oscillator pin, or the input for a single-ended clock (20 MHz or 40 MHz) at VIO levels. A series resistor sits between this pin and a crystal.

pins.name: nWKRQ
pins.function: Wake request, active low. Push-pull from an internal 3.6 V rail by default, kept alive in sleep; set to work from VIO it becomes open drain and needs a pull-up to VIO.

pins.name: GPIO1
pins.function: Pin whose job is set over SPI: an output (by default the M_CAN interrupt line 1, active low) or a watchdog trigger input. In test mode it carries TXD_INT_PHY or RXD_INT_CAN in.

pins.name: SCLK
pins.function: SPI clock from the host. Weak internal pull-up.

pins.name: SDI
pins.function: SPI data in, from the host's controller output. Weak internal pull-up.

pins.name: SDO
pins.function: SPI data out to the host. High impedance while nCS is high; shows the global fault flag as soon as nCS falls.

pins.name: nCS
pins.function: SPI chip select, active low. Weak internal pull-up keeps the part deselected.

pins.name: nINT
pins.function: Global interrupt to the host, active low, open drain; needs a pull-up to VIO. Low while any unmasked flag in 0x0820 or 0x0824 is set. In test mode it is the EN_INT input.

pins.name: GPO2
pins.function: Open-drain output whose job is set over SPI (M_CAN interrupt line 0, watchdog output, or a copy of nINT); needs a pull-up to VIO. In test mode it carries RXD_INT_PHY or TXD_INT_CAN out.

pins.name: CANL
pins.function: CAN bus low line.

pins.name: CANH
pins.function: CAN bus high line.

pins.name: WAKE
pins.function: Local wake-up input, rated to 42 V, triggered on rising, falling or either edge. Wants 10 nF to ground when routed off the board; tie to VSUP or GND when not used.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground. Soldered to the ground plane together with the thermal pad.

pins.name: VSUP
pins.function: Battery supply for all internal regulators, the transceiver and VCCOUT. 100 nF at the pin.

pins.name: INH
pins.function: Inhibit output, VSUP less a diode drop, for the enable input of the node's regulator. On in every mode but sleep, where it floats. Not a power output and not reverse-battery protected; may be left open when unused.

pins.name: VCCOUT
pins.function: Output of the internal 5 V regulator that also feeds the transceiver. 10 µF placed at the pin.

pins.name: VIO
pins.function: Logic supply, 3.3 V or 5 V, for the SPI pins, GPIO1, GPO2 and the oscillator. 100 nF at the pin.

pins.name: FLTR
pins.function: Filter node of the internal digital core regulator; 300 nF or more to ground.

pins.name: RST
pins.function: Reset. Weak internal pull-down. A high pulse longer than tPULSE_WIDTH gives a power-on reset and leaves the part in standby.

pins.name: OSC2
pins.function: Crystal oscillator pin. Grounded when a single-ended clock drives OSC1.

pins.name: Thermal pad
pins.function: Exposed pad; soldered to ground.

circuits.title: Typical application, 3.3 V MCU and crystal
circuits.description: A 3.3 V microcontroller node with its CAN FD port on the TCAN4550-Q1. The battery passes a series diode onto the VSUP rail, which feeds VSUP (10 µF on the rail, 100 nF at the pin) and the input of the 3.3 V regulator; INH drives the regulator's enable, so the node's supply switches off in sleep and comes back on a wake. The regulator output is both the MCU supply and VIO. FLTR has 330 nF and VCCOUT 10 µF. A switch to ground on the WAKE network (3 kΩ pull-up from VSUP, 10 nF filter, 33 kΩ into WAKE) gives a local wake-up. The MCU drives the SPI pins and RST, and reads nWKRQ, nINT, GPO2 and GPIO1 on its GPIO pins. A 40 MHz crystal with load capacitors sits on OSC1 and OSC2. CANH and CANL go to the two-wire bus.

An optional terminating node and optional filtering, transient and ESD parts sit on CANH and CANL.
Decoupling capacitors are added as needed.

circuits.title: Typical application, 3.3 V MCU with clock from the MCU
circuits.description: The same 3.3 V node as the crystal version, but the TCAN4550-Q1 takes its clock from the MCU: the MCU runs its own 20 MHz crystal and its CLKOUT drives OSC1, while OSC2 is grounded. A 20 MHz clock supports CAN FD at 2 Mbps; 40 MHz is recommended for 5 Mbps. Supply, wake, SPI and interrupt wiring are unchanged.

circuits.title: Standard termination
circuits.description: A single resistor equal to the cable's 120 Ω characteristic impedance across CANH and CANL, at a node that ends the bus.

circuits.title: Split termination
circuits.description: The termination as two equal halves, RTERM/2 each, in series across CANH and CANL with CSPLIT from their midpoint to ground. It filters the bus common mode and stops it jumping at the start and end of each message, which lowers emissions.
notes: RTERM is 120 Ω, the cable's characteristic impedance.

operation.text: A CAN FD controller (Bosch M_CAN, ISO 11898-1:2015) and a CAN FD transceiver (ISO 11898-2:2016) in one package, reached from a host processor over SPI at up to 18 MHz. It lets a processor without CAN FD, or without enough CAN ports, run classic CAN and CAN FD frames, with data rates up to 8 Mbps.

Recessive (logic high, the idle state): the bus floats at 2.5 V common mode through each receiver's high-value input resistors. Dominant (logic low): one or more drivers push current through the terminations, making a differential voltage; dominant overrides recessive, and several nodes driving at once during arbitration give a larger differential. In the low-power modes the bus pins are weakly biased to ground instead.

Many limits refer to TXD_INT, RXD_INT and EN_INT, the internal links between controller and transceiver that stand in for a stand-alone transceiver's pins. A test mode brings either the transceiver side (TXD/RXD_INT_PHY) or the controller side (TXD/RXD_INT_CAN) out to GPIO1, GPO2 and nINT for compliance testing.
Battery input feeding the internal regulators for the digital core, the transceiver and VCCOUT. 100 nF at the pin. At power-up VSUP must climb past the UVSUP rising threshold.
Sets the logic levels of the SPI pins, GPIO1 and GPO2 to match the host (3.3 V to 5 V ±5 %), so no level shifter is needed, and powers the oscillator. 100 nF at the pin.

The internal 5 V LDO supplies both the transceiver and VCCOUT, 125 mA in total; what is left for VCCOUT depends on the transceiver's draw, and during a bus fault that takes the whole LDO, VCCOUT gets nothing. The LDO is off in sleep. 10 µF as close to the pin as possible.
Both go to a ground plane, which also carries the heat away.

High-voltage output at VSUP minus a diode drop, meant for the enable pin of the node's high-voltage regulator. It is on in every mode except sleep, where it goes high impedance so the whole node can drop to its lowest power. Disable it with 0x0800[9] = 1, or leave it open if unused; a 100 kΩ pull-down can discharge it when it is high-Z. It is a logic-level signal, not a power output, is not reverse-battery protected, and is not to leave the module.

High-voltage local wake input. By default either edge wakes the part; 0x0800[31:30] can set rising only, falling only or off. Routed off-board it wants 10 nF to ground; unused, tie it to VSUP or GND. Internal bias follows the pin state (pull-up to VSUP when high, pull-down when low) to save current, which can look like a wake event at power-up. The wake filter time is tWAKE; local wake works in sleep and standby, not normal.
Filter capacitor for the internal digital core regulator: 300 nF minimum to ground (330 nF typical).

Weak internal pull-down. Pulsing RST high for longer than tPULSE_WIDTH and back low gives a power-on reset: registers go to default and the part lands in standby. From normal or standby, INH and nWKRQ stay on; from sleep, they turn on as standby is entered. Wait at least 700 µs after a reset before any SPI access.

Crystal pins, or OSC1 alone as a single-ended clock input at VIO level with OSC2 grounded. A 40 MHz crystal or clock is recommended for CAN FD; 20 MHz is the minimum and supports 2 Mbps. Either needs ±0.5 % accuracy. Crystal load capacitors and the series (damping) resistor need care; TI's TCAN455x clock optimization application note covers their choice. The part was evaluated with NX2016SA 20 MHz and 40 MHz crystals. The frequency in use is entered in 0x0800[27].

Wake request output for a wake from the bus (WUP), the WAKE pin (LWU) or power-on. By default it is pulled low and latched on a wake, to enable a regulator that does not use INH; with 0x0800[8] = 1 it acts as an interrupt that releases when the wake flag is cleared. It runs from an internal 3.6 V rail that stays alive in sleep, or from VIO (0x0800[19]), in which case it is open drain, needs a pull-up to VIO and asserts only once VIO is stable; the rail choice survives sleep. It is the OR of the unmasked CANINT, LWU and WKERR flags. A pull-up on this pin requires the VIO setting.
Open-drain global interrupt, needs a pull-up to VIO; low while any unmasked fault in 0x0820 or 0x0824 is set. In test mode it becomes EN_INT: high = normal, low = standby.

Defaults to the M_CAN_INT 1 interrupt output (active low). 0x0800[15:14] = 00 makes it a general output whose signal is chosen in 0x0800[11:10]; = 10 makes it the watchdog trigger input. In test mode (0x0800[21] = 1) it is the transceiver's TXD_INT_PHY input or the controller's RXD_INT_CAN input, chosen by 0x0800[0].
Open-drain configurable output for selected interrupts, needs a pull-up to VIO; set by 0x0800[23:22], including a watchdog output. In test mode it outputs RXD_INT_PHY or TXD_INT_CAN.

Normal, standby and sleep are chosen over SPI; two protected modes (TSD and UVIO) are modified standby modes entered to protect the part or the bus. The only change the part makes on its own is sleep to standby on a WUP or LWU.

Driver and receiver fully active: TXD_INT from the controller becomes a differential signal on CANH/CANL and the bus is read back onto RXD_INT. After an undervoltage event has cleared, its interrupt flags must be cleared before normal mode can be entered.

Driver off and the normal receiver ignored; the low-power receiver watches for a wake-up pattern, the WAKE monitor runs, SPI works, INH stays on and nWKRQ is low by default. Everything else is at lowest power. Only one wake interrupt (LWU or CANINT) is raised per standby entry, so bus traffic cannot flood the host. Entering standby at power-up, after a power-on reset or after a wake from sleep starts tINACTIVE (about four minutes): the host must clear the interrupt flags or select normal mode before it runs out or the part sleeps. SWE_DIS (0x0800[1]) turns this off for wakes from sleep but not for power-up or reset.

Like standby but with SPI and INH off; the low-power receiver runs from VSUP and nWKRQ from an internal rail, so VIO may be switched off and the host still gets a wake signal. Register and message RAM power is removed, so the part must be configured again before normal mode. Only a wake event, a RST pulse or a power cycle leaves sleep. 0x0820[23] (SMS) is set if a fault, not a command, caused sleep. A UVCCOUT interrupt can appear while the LDO shuts down on the way into sleep; ignore it or mask it with 0x0830[22] first.

In sleep the low-power receiver and bus monitor stay on and the bus pins are weakly pulled to ground. A wake-up pattern is a filtered dominant, then a filtered recessive, then a filtered dominant, each longer than tWK_FILTER, all within tWK_TIMEOUT; other traffic in between does not reset the monitor. After it, every filtered dominant drives RXD_INT low (bus wake via RXD request), the part moves to standby and raises nINT and nWKRQ. Bus states shorter than tWK_FILTER(min) never count, longer than tWK_FILTER(max) always count, and those between may. Going to normal mode or an undervoltage on VCC drops the BWRR state.
A transition on WAKE in either direction (by default) with a switch to VSUP or ground is a local wake request; it is filtered by tWAKE(min) and moves the part from sleep to standby.

Four configurations. With 0x0800[21] = 1, 0x0800[0] = 0 maps the transceiver's TXD_INT_PHY to GPIO1, RXD_INT_PHY to GPO2 and EN_INT to nINT; 0x0800[0] = 1 maps the controller's RXD_INT_CAN to GPIO1 and TXD_INT_CAN to GPO2. The other two are the M_CAN internal and external loop-back modes, set in the M_CAN registers over SPI.

Relies on the SWE (sleep wake error) timer to judge whether the host is alive. SWE is on by default (SWE_DIS = 0) and a power-on reset turns it back on; the failsafe feature itself is off by default and enabled with 0x0800[13]. Three cases send the part to sleep: at power-up the host has tINACTIVE to clear PWRON or select normal mode (this one cannot be disabled); with failsafe on, after a wake from sleep the host has the same time to clear the flags and select normal; and with failsafe on, if CANSLNT persists for tINACTIVE in standby or normal (lost clock, dead host, missed sleep command). After a wake back to standby, tSILENCE and tINACTIVE restart.

On by default with four periods (60 ms, 600 ms, 3 s, 6 s); runs in normal and standby, off in sleep. It does not start until the first trigger, a 1 written to 0x0800[18] or an edge on GPIO1 set as watchdog input; with no first trigger it stays disabled. A timeout can raise an interrupt, pulse INH and drop to standby, or pulse the watchdog output pin (GPO2), chosen in 0x0800[17:16]; the interrupt flag is always set. The clock frequency must be entered in 0x0800[27]. In UVIO protected mode the timer is held in reset and resumes in standby; after a sleep command it stops. To change any watchdog setting, disable it, change it, then enable it again.

TXD_INT and RXD_INT behave like a transceiver's TXD and RXD with CMOS levels referred to VIO. In normal mode the receiver threshold is 0.5 V to 0.9 V differential; in standby and sleep the low-power receiver uses 0.4 V to 1.15 V.

A falling edge on TXD_INT starts the timer; if no rising edge comes within tTXD_INT_DTO the driver turns off, freeing the bus for other nodes, and it comes back when TXD_INT goes recessive. The receiver keeps working and the bus is biased recessive during the fault. It can be exercised in test mode by holding GPIO1 dominant and watching GPO2.

The driver limits current into a shorted bus line, and the dominant timeout stops the higher dominant short-circuit current from lasting. Because CAN forces recessive bits (stuffing, control fields, interframe space), the average current is set by the dominant/recessive mix (see the equation).

Above the shutdown threshold the internal 5 V LDO turns off, cutting the transmit path and VCCOUT; the TSD flag is set and an interrupt raised, and other flags (a bus short to battery, say) may also set. SPI and the digital core keep working. After about 300 ms the junction is checked again and the part returns to standby once the fault has gone. In TSD protected mode writes selecting normal or standby are ignored; a sleep write is accepted. A TSD during a VIO undervoltage sends the part to sleep.

When VSUP falls to UVSUP the 5 V regulator can no longer hold up: UVCCOUT is flagged, the regulator turns off and the transceiver goes to a standby state. If VSUP recovers the part enters standby; if it falls on to the power-on reset level everything shuts down and the part restarts as from power-up, registers cleared.

Below UVIO the transceiver, the clock circuits and the host I/O stop, and the tUV timer starts. If VIO is still low when it expires the part goes to sleep, losing the UVIO flag with the registers; a wake then brings it to standby with INH on, and the cycle repeats while VIO stays low. In UVIO protected mode the clock is lost, the digital core resets and the M_CAN must be programmed again.
With no supply the bus pins and logic pins leak very little, so an unpowered node does not load a working bus or other powered circuits. The UVLO circuits watch both rising and falling rails.

On a UVIO, UVCCOUT or TSD fault, and on every change from normal to standby, the part writes CCCR.INIT = 1, halting pending transmit and receive work; on returning to normal it writes CCCR.INIT = 0 and pending messages (TXBRP bits) go out automatically. After an undervoltage clears, allow tMODE_CHANGE before sending or receiving.

On going bus-off the M_CAN sets CCCR.INIT itself. After the host clears INIT it waits for 129 bus-idle sequences of 11 recessive bits before resuming; each sequence writes a Bit0Error to PSR.LEC and is counted in ECR.REC, so the host can watch the recovery. Toggling INIT cannot shorten it.

Access is in 32-bit words. 2 KB of message RAM (MRAM, the Bosch M_CAN message RAM, not magnetic RAM) is freely split into Tx and Rx buffers and FIFOs. Its contents and ECC are unknown at power-up, so it should be zeroed after power-up, a power-on reset and every wake from sleep; at minimum write two words (8 bytes) of payload to any Tx buffer element even when the DLC is smaller, or a BEU error puts the M_CAN into initialization.

Mode 0 (CPOL = 0, CPHA = 0): SDI is sampled on SCLK rising edges and SDO changes on falling edges. Each transaction is a command byte, two address bytes and a length byte, then the data words; SDO starts with the global status byte, then shows register contents (for a write, the contents before the write). A write takes effect only after exactly a multiple of 32 bits and the rising edge of nCS; otherwise the last word is dropped and SPIERR is set. Because of the 32-bit rule the part belongs on a shared bus with its own nCS, not in a daisy chain. With nCS high SDO is high impedance; on nCS falling it immediately shows the global fault flag, which is also the first bit out.

0x0000 to 0x000C: device ID and SPI registers. 0x0800 to 0x083C: configuration and interrupt flags. 0x1000 to 0x10FC: M_CAN. 0x8000 to 0x87FF: message RAM. Addresses are word aligned and bits [1:0] are ignored (0x1004 to 0x1007 all reach 0x1004); only the low 16 address bits count. MRAM start addresses are entered without the 0x8000 prefix.

A typical CAN bus is up to 40 m with stubs up to 0.3 m; careful design, lower data rates and other system standards (ARINC825, CANopen, DeviceNet, SAE J2284, SAE J1939, NMEA200) allow more, such as CANopen's 1 km with under 64 nodes. The driver meets 1.5 V differential into 50 Ω to 65 Ω and 1.4 V into 45 Ω.

The bus is a single twisted pair, shielded or not, of 120 Ω characteristic impedance, terminated at both ends with its characteristic impedance; stubs stay as short as possible. A termination inside a node is generally not recommended if the node can be removed. Split termination (two halves with a capacitor to ground) steadies the common mode and lowers emissions.

In normal mode the bus is biased to 2.5 V. In the low-power modes the part uses automatic biasing: the bias stays off (bus near ground) until bus activity of the wake-up pattern kind is seen, turns on, and turns off again once tSILENCE expires with the part in a low-power mode.

If VSUP sags below its operating range and recovers: UVSUP falls at about 4.7 V and rises at about 5.5 V; the digital core enters reset near 3.6 V and leaves it near 4.25 V, after which every register is back at default and must be programmed again. INH switches off somewhere between 1.42 V and 3.14 V and on between 1.67 V and 4.15 V across process, voltage and temperature.

Works with 3.3 V and 5 V hosts by taking VIO from the host's regulator. Designed for ISO 11898 bus loads of 50 Ω to 65 Ω. For data rates to 8 Mbps use a 40 MHz crystal and keep the host-to-part traces short and matched. Budget the 5 V LDO for the transceiver plus up to 70 mA on VCCOUT. Given the temperature and input range, a high-k board with good heat spreading is recommended; with 70 mA on VCCOUT, a dominant 60 Ω bus and 125 °C ambient, thermal shutdown can begin near VSUP = 20 V (19 V with a 50 Ω load), after which ISUP settles near 74.5 mA as the part cycles through standby.

Runs from the battery; internal regulators supply the controller, transceiver and low-voltage receiver, and the SPI and GPIO run from VIO. Place bulk capacitance on VSUP and VIO as the system needs, 100 nF near the VSUP and VIO pins, at least 300 nF on FLTR and at least 10 µF on VCCOUT. Choose values so ageing never takes them below these minimums; more may be needed.

Put TVS diodes (bidirectional TVS or varistor, D1), optional bus filter capacitors and the common-mode choke near the bus connector, in line with the signal path, so transients are stopped before they reach the board; on-chip IEC ESD protection is high, but external TVS raises system immunity. ESD and transients span roughly 3 MHz to 3 GHz, so use high-frequency layout: supply and ground planes, and at least two vias on each bypass and protection part connection. Bypass and bulk capacitors go as close as possible to the FLTR, VIO, VCCOUT and VSUP pins. Split termination with its centre tap to ground through a capacitor provides common-mode filtering. nINT and GPO2 need pull-ups of 2 kΩ to 10 kΩ to VIO. WAKE uses 10 nF to ground with 33 kΩ in series and 3 kΩ to the switch. INH may float or take a 100 kΩ pull-down. A crystal needs a series resistor at pin 1, and the OSC1 and OSC2 traces should be matched in length.
